--- title: "k-nearest neighbours" description: "k-nearest neighbours predicts a new station from the training stations most like it, with no shape assumed. How many to average decides between copying noise and blurring the pattern, and on the survey an assumed curve still predicts new sites better." order: 4 categories: [supervised, regression, classification] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Similar stations have similar counts Every model so far in this section has a formula: a weighted sum of the inputs, passed through a function that keeps the prediction in range. k-nearest neighbours has none. [Types of learning](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) used it to predict for a new station from the 15 survey stations most like it. It keeps the training data and, for each new station, finds the *k* closest ones and averages their answers: their mean count for a regression, or for presence the share of them where the species was found. That share is a probability, like logistic regression's, and a threshold turns it into yes or no. Because nothing about the shape is assumed, the neighbours can follow a peak, a step or anything else, as long as enough stations lie close by. "Closest" is a distance across all the inputs at once, so each input is first standardised, as [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) explains; otherwise the input with the largest numbers would choose the neighbours. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The number of neighbours sets how smooth the predictions are With $k = 1$, each prediction copies a single station, chance highs and lows included. Every training station is its own nearest neighbour, so the model reproduces its training data exactly and predicts new stations badly. Fitting the training data so closely that predictions on new data get worse is **overfitting**, which [Underfitting and overfitting](../05-generalisation/underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) covers in full. At the other end, with $k$ equal to the whole training set, every prediction is the same average and the inputs are ignored. Larger $k$ smooths more. $k$ is a **hyperparameter**: a setting fixed before the model is fitted, not learned from the data. The training error cannot choose it, since that always favours $k = 1$, so it is chosen on validation data, the role [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) set aside for choosing between models. ## Beyond the data, the prediction levels off For a station warmer than any in the training data, the nearest stations are the warmest ones there, and they stay the same however much warmer it gets. The prediction levels off at the edge of the data: it never turns negative, as a polynomial can, but it cannot carry a trend on either. [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) deals with predicting outside the data. ::: {.diagram} ![k-nearest neighbours predicts from the k nearest examples. One neighbour follows every chance high and low; all of them give one average everywhere. Past the last example the neighbours never change, so the prediction levels off.](img/nearest-neighbours.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Neighbours, the k nearest examples: a scatter of grey points on input 1 against input 2, with a new example in the middle; the five points closest to it are blue, joined to it by thin lines and ringed by a circle. The prediction is their average, or the share of each category. Number of neighbours, k sets the smoothness: points scatter around a hump against one input; with k = 1 the prediction is a jagged line that jumps to every point, with k = 7 it is a smooth hump, and with k = all it is a dashed flat line at the average. Beyond the data, flat at the edges: a smooth line rises and falls through the data, then stays level in shaded regions with no data at either end. A note says distance treats every input alike, so the inputs are put on one scale first."} ::: ## Worked example The data and the split by site are those of the earlier pages. The training stations are split once more by site, into fitting and validation sites, for choosing $k$. The recipe fills the gaps, turns seabed type and season into 0/1 columns and standardises every column, so that each counts alike in the distance. The model needs no squared terms: the neighbours find a peak, if there is one, by themselves. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) fit_split <- group_initial_split(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) fitting <- training(fit_split) validation <- testing(fit_split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season knn_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.base import clone from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] inner = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) fit_rows, val_rows = next(inner.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) fitting, validation = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[val_rows] # The dropped level of each category is the first, as in R: gravel and spring. knn_recipe = Pipeline([ ("columns", ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop=["gravel", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ])), ("standardise", StandardScaler()), ]) ``` ::: ::: ### Validation sites choose the number of neighbours In tidymodels the model is `nearest_neighbor()`, which uses the kknn package; in scikit-learn it is `KNeighborsRegressor`. kknn gives closer neighbours more weight unless told otherwise, so `weight_func = "rectangular"` makes every neighbour count equally, as scikit-learn does by default. Models with $k$ from 1 to 300 are fitted on the fitting sites and scored with the [RMSE](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#rmse-measures-a-typical-miss-on-the-test-stations), the typical miss in animals, on the stations they were fitted to and on the validation sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knn_model <- function(k) { nearest_neighbor(neighbors = k, weight_func = "rectangular") |> set_mode("regression") } score_k <- function(k) { fitted <- workflow(knn_recipe, knn_model(k)) |> fit(fitting) error <- function(data) { rmse_vec(data$abundance, predict(fitted, data)$.pred) } tibble(k = k, training = error(fitting), validation = error(validation)) } ks <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 70, 100, 150, 200, 300) neighbours <- map(ks, score_k) |> list_rbind() neighbours |> slice_min(validation) |> mutate(across(-k, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| k| training| validation| |--:|--------:|----------:| | 30| 4.59| 3.91|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def knn_model(k, data): return Pipeline([ ("recipe", clone(knn_recipe)), ("model", KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k)), ]).fit(data[predictors], data["abundance"]) def rmse(fitted, data): return root_mean_squared_error(data["abundance"], fitted.predict(data[predictors])) rows = [] for k in [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 70, 100, 150, 200, 300]: fitted = knn_model(k, fitting) rows.append({"k": k, "training": rmse(fitted, fitting), "validation": rmse(fitted, validation)}) neighbours = pd.DataFrame(rows) neighbours.loc[[neighbours["validation"].idxmin()]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | k | training | validation | |----:|-----------:|-------------:| | 50 | 3.91 | 4.61 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} best_k <- neighbours |> slice_min(validation) |> pull(k) neighbours |> pivot_longer(c(training, validation), names_to = "data", values_to = "rmse") |> ggplot(aes(k, rmse, colour = data)) + geom_vline(xintercept = best_k, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(training = ml_palette[["blue"]], validation = ml_palette[["orange"]]), breaks = c("training", "validation"), labels = c("Fitting stations", "Validation sites")) + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300)) + expand_limits(y = 0) + labs(x = "Number of neighbours, k", y = "RMSE (individuals)", colour = NULL, title = "One neighbour copies its own stations; hundreds blur the pattern") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The RMSE of k-nearest neighbours for each number of neighbours, on the stations it was fitted to and on the validation sites. The number of neighbours is on a log scale, and the dashed line marks the lowest validation error.](nearest-neighbours_files/figure-html/fig-neighbours-1.png){#fig-neighbours fig-alt='Two lines of RMSE against the number of neighbours from 1 to 300 on a log scale. The training line starts at zero for one neighbour and rises steadily. The validation line starts high, falls quickly over the first few values, is nearly flat through the middle, with its lowest point marked by a dashed line, and rises again towards 300.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: With one neighbour the training error is 0, since every fitting station predicts its own count, but the validation error is 5.16, the worst of all. The validation error falls to 3.91 at $k$ = 30, then rises again to 4.31 at 300, where each prediction averages over stations that are no longer alike. The curve is flat around its lowest point: every $k$ from 15 to 70 comes within 0.05 of it, so the exact choice matters little. Past a few neighbours the validation error sits below the training error only because the counts at the validation sites happen to vary less: their standard deviation is 4.34, against 5.18 at the fitting sites. ### Poisson regression predicts new sites better than k-nearest neighbours The neighbours are refitted at $k$ = 30 on all the training stations and scored once on the test sites, beside Poisson regression from [Regression for counts](count-regression.qmd), with its squared depth and temperature. [$R^2$](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd#one-linear-regression-shows-each-kind) is the share of the variation in the test counts that the predictions follow. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knn_fit <- workflow(knn_recipe, knn_model(best_k)) |> fit(train) curve_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) poisson_fit <- workflow(curve_recipe, poisson_reg()) |> fit(train) score <- function(fitted, label) { predicted <- predict(fitted, test)$.pred tibble(model = label, rmse = rmse_vec(test$abundance, predicted), rsq = rsq_trad_vec(test$abundance, predicted)) } scores <- bind_rows(score(knn_fit, "k-nearest neighbours"), score(poisson_fit, "Poisson regression")) scores |> mutate(across(-model, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | rmse| rsq| |:--------------------|----:|----:| |k-nearest neighbours | 3.83| 0.10| |Poisson regression | 3.55| 0.23|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures best_k = int(neighbours.loc[neighbours["validation"].idxmin(), "k"]) knn_fit = knn_model(best_k, train) def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop=["gravel", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) poisson_fit = Pipeline([ ("recipe", curve_recipe), ("model", PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, solver="newton-cholesky")), ]).fit(train[predictors], train["abundance"]) def score(fitted, label): predicted = fitted.predict(test[predictors]) return {"model": label, "rmse": root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], predicted), "rsq": r2_score(test["abundance"], predicted)} pd.DataFrame([score(knn_fit, "k-nearest neighbours"), score(poisson_fit, "Poisson regression")]).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | rmse | rsq | |:---------------------|-------:|------:| | k-nearest neighbours | 5.05 | 0.16 | | Poisson regression | 4.82 | 0.23 | ::: ::: ::: k-nearest neighbours misses by 3.83 animals on the test sites, with an $R^2$ of 0.10; Poisson regression misses by 3.55, with 0.23. Poisson regression assumes a shape, a smooth curve in each input, and fits it to every training station at once. The neighbours assume nothing and learn from the 30 stations nearest each new one. With six inputs, even the nearest stations differ from the new one in several of them, so their average blurs what each input does. Freedom from a shape pays when stations are plentiful and the relationship has a shape no formula expects; on this survey the assumed curve wins. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - k-nearest neighbours predicts from the *k* most similar training stations, measured on standardised inputs, and assumes no shape. - One neighbour copies chance highs and lows; very many blur the pattern into one average. *k* is a hyperparameter, chosen on validation sites, never on the training error. - Beyond the data the neighbours stop changing, so the predictions level off. - On the survey's test sites, Poisson regression's assumed curve predicts better than the neighbours: flexibility needs many stations close by. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Change the outcome to `present` and the mode to `"classification"`, choose $k$ on the validation sites with `accuracy_vec()`, and compare the test accuracy with the one on [Logistic regression](logistic-regression.qmd). 2. Refit the neighbours with depth and temperature as the only inputs and choose $k$ again. Does the validation error improve? With fewer inputs to match, how much nearer are the neighbours?
